Preached Word
PREECHED WURD
noun phrase
From Old English præcan (to preach, proclaim, from Latin praedicare—prae- before + dicare to proclaim) + Old English word (speech, utterance, the Word). The compound names the proclaimed Scripture as the central instrument of the Spirit’s saving and sanctifying work—the Word of God not merely read or studied but publicly, authoritatively, and expositorily declared in the congregation.

Biblical Definition

The preached Word is the publicly proclaimed Scripture, declared by an ordained minister of the gospel before the assembled church as the Spirit’s primary instrument for the conversion of sinners and the edification of saints. The Reformed tradition identifies the preached Word as the chief among the means of grace: it is through the “foolishness of the message preached” that God is pleased to save those who believe (1 Cor. 1:21), and faith itself comes “by the word of Christ” heard through the preacher (Rom. 10:17). The preached Word is not a merely human performance: it is God’s own speech through an instrument. Isaiah 55:11 establishes this sovereignty: “My word…shall not return to Me void, but it shall accomplish what I please.” Paul’s commission to Timothy is the paradigm for the ministry of the preached Word: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.” (2 Tim. 4:2). The act of preaching is the act of Scripture speaking: the preacher is not the origin of the message but its herald, reading, explaining, and applying the Word of God to the consciences of those assembled. The Second Helvetic Confession (1566) captures the Reformed consensus: “The preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God.” This is not a claim that every sermon is inerrant but that when the Scripture is faithfully proclaimed, God Himself addresses the congregation through His Word. Corporate worship in the Reformed tradition is therefore ordered around the preached Word: the Directory for Public Worship, the Westminster Standards, and the 1689 Confession all place preaching at the center of the Lord’s Day service.

Webster 1828 Definition

Preached Word: the publicly proclaimed Scripture, declared by an ordained minister as the Spirit’s chief instrument of conversion and edification; not a human opinion about God but God’s own authoritative address to the assembled congregation through His herald.

expand to see more

PREACH, verb transitive. To proclaim, publish, or openly make known; in the sacred sense, to deliver a public discourse on a religious subject; to announce the gospel of Christ to men, holding forth the doctrines and promises of Scripture and applying them to the conscience and heart.

2. (Reformed theology) The preached Word as the first and chief means of grace: through hearing the Word proclaimed, faith is generated (Rom. 10:17), sinners are converted (Acts 2:37–41), and saints are built up in holiness (Eph. 4:11–12). No ordinance supplements or supplants the preached Word; the Lord’s Supper itself is a visible preaching of the Lord’s death.

3. The authority of the preached Word: the preacher speaks not on his own authority but under the authority of the Scripture he expounds. His obligation is faithfulness to the text; his hearers’ obligation is the Berean test (Acts 17:11)—to receive what is scriptural and reject what is not.

4. Preached Word vs. read Word: the Reformed tradition distinguishes but does not separate these. Public reading of Scripture is itself a means of grace (1 Tim. 4:13); preaching adds exposition and application, making the Word accessible to the conscience in its contemporary force.

Key Scripture

2 Timothy 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

Romans 10:17 — "So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God."

Isaiah 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

1 Corinthians 1:21 — "For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe."

Modern Corruption

Entertainment-driven, experiential, and therapeutic models of worship have displaced the preached Word from the center of Reformed worship, replacing authoritative biblical proclamation with storytelling, self-help application, and emotional manipulation.

expand to see more

The seeker-sensitive movement (Bill Hybels, Willow Creek; Rick Warren, Saddleback) deliberately reduced the length, doctrinal density, and confrontational character of preaching in order to lower the offense of the gospel to unchurched hearers. The strategy produced numerical growth at the cost of doctrinal substance: congregations reared on “felt need” preaching are trained to receive the Bible as a resource for personal fulfillment rather than as the sovereign address of God to sinners. The preacher becomes a life-coach dispensing therapeutic wisdom, and the sermon becomes a self-help lecture with biblical garnish. This is not the preached Word of Reformed confessionalism; it is the preacher’s word about what God can do for you—a fundamentally different genre.

The charismatic and New Apostolic Reformation traditions displace the preached Word from the center of corporate worship by prioritizing direct prophetic revelation, extended musical worship, and apostolic “impartation” as the primary channels of divine encounter. On this model, the sermon is one element among many spiritual experiences rather than the normative and supreme means of grace. Scripture’s own testimony is against this: faith comes “by the word of” (Rom. 10:17), not by atmosphere, musical intensity, or prophetic utterance. The Spirit’s self-appointed instrument is the proclaimed Word—the “sword of the Spirit” (Eph. 6:17)—and worship structures that marginalize it marginalize the Spirit’s own chosen weapon.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin praedicare (to proclaim publicly) and the Hebrew concept of the nabi (prophet as forth-teller) converge on the Reformed understanding of the preached Word: the minister is a herald, proclaiming not his own counsel but the authoritative Word of the King.

expand to see more

Latin praedicare — to proclaim publicly before an audience; root of “preach”—the preacher stands before the congregation as a herald (kērux) of the divine decree, not as an expert sharing personal insights

Greek kēryssein — to herald, proclaim, cry out; the NT word for preaching (Matt. 4:17; Rom. 10:14)—the herald’s authority is derived entirely from the King whose message he carries

Hebrew nabi — prophet, forth-teller; the OT prophet speaks not his own word but the word given by God (“Thus says the LORD”); the NT preacher stands in this tradition as an expositor of the completed canon

Greek logos — word, reason, discourse; John 1:14’s use of logos for Christ Himself establishes the theological weight of “the Word”—the preached word participates in the authority of the incarnate Word it proclaims

Latin applicatio — application, bringing to bear; the Puritan tradition insisted that faithful preaching must include applicatio—bringing the text’s truth to bear on the specific condition, sin, comfort, and duty of the hearer

Usage

"The Westminster Directory for Public Worship (1645) specifies that the preached Word is the pinnacle of Lord’s Day worship: the minister is to preach “painfully [i.e., diligently], not lazily or slightly,” with doctrine, reason, and use (application) in order, and the people are to attend “with diligence, preparation, and prayer”."

"The principle that “it is in the preached Word that the elect are called” (1689 Confession 14.1) grounds the church’s missionary obligation: if saving faith comes by hearing (Rom. 10:17), then wherever there is no preacher there is no ordinary means for faith to arise, and the church must send preachers (Rom. 10:14–15)."

"Charles Spurgeon’s famous remark that the Bible is like a lion—“you don’t defend it, you let it loose”—is a summary theology of the preached Word: the preacher’s task is faithful exposition, not rhetorical apologetics; the Word defends itself by the Spirit’s power."
